# Reader evaluation (Principle 4)

ISO 24495-1:2023 requires evaluation with actual readers before a document is considered plain. This file describes how to run that evaluation and gives templates you can reuse.

## Why it matters

The four principles are interdependent. You can follow the guidelines for relevance, findability, and understandability, but only real readers can confirm that the document is usable. Without reader testing, the document has been drafted in plain language — not proven to be plain language.

## How much testing is enough

Test with at least one representative reader per audience group. Two is better. Five per group is diminishing returns for most documents.

You do not need statistical power. You need to see where readers pause, ask questions, or misread.

## Three methods

### Method 1 — Findability test (5 minutes per reader)

Send the reader the document and ask three questions:

1. Read only the headings. What do you think this document is asking you to do?
2. Now open the document. Can you find your section in under 30 seconds?
3. Was anything hard to find?

### Method 2 — Comprehension test (15 minutes per reader)

Send the reader the document and ask them to read it. Then ask:

1. In one sentence, what is this document asking you to do?
2. What decision do you need to make?
3. What is not clear?
4. Was there any word you had to look up or guess at?
5. Anything you disagree with?

### Method 3 — Think-aloud (30 minutes per reader)

Meet with the reader on a call. Share your screen with the document open. Ask them to read it aloud and narrate their reactions. Record if they consent. Do not interrupt except to unstick.

Watch for:

- Where they slow down.
- Where they scroll back.
- Where they ask a question the document should have answered.
- Where they misread something.
- What they say when they finish. Do they know what to do next?

Method 3 gives the most signal. Method 1 gives the least effort. Method 2 is the default.

## Templates

### Slack DM template — Method 2

> Hi [name],
>
> I've drafted a document that will affect [team / topic]. Before I send it out for real, I'd like 15 minutes of your time to check it works.
>
> Please read [link] and reply with:
>
> 1. In one sentence, what is this document asking you to do?
> 2. What decision would you need to make?
> 3. What is not clear?
> 4. Any word you had to look up or guess?
> 5. Anything you disagree with?
>
> Thanks — I'll revise based on what you tell me before sending it out.

### Meeting invite template — Method 3

> **Title:** Read-through of [doc name] (30 min)
>
> **Body:** I want to know if this document works before I send it out. On the call I'll share my screen with the document open. Please read it aloud and tell me what you're thinking as you go. I'll take notes and revise afterward.
>
> No prep needed. Coffee is optional.

## Revising after the test

Group the feedback:

- **Fix immediately** — anything a reader could not find, understand, or use.
- **Consider** — subjective preferences that do not affect the four principles.
- **Ignore politely** — feedback that would break the document for the primary audience.

Send a short thank-you and, if you can, one line about how you changed the document based on their feedback. This makes them more likely to help next time.

## Continuing evaluation after publishing

For long-lived documents:

- Add a "How to leave feedback" section at the end.
- Review the document every 6 or 12 months.
- Update when reader context changes (new team, new tools, new regulation).
